Gainesville, a college town in north-central Florida, briefly had an experimental renewable-energy policy that attracted global attention.
And now that it has wound down the program, started in early 2009, others are wondering what it can teach about the role of solar energy in the broader US electricity market.
Under the FIT, as it is called, Gainesville Regional Utilities (GRU), the city-owned power company, offered anyone who installed solar panels a guaranteed price for every kilowatt-hour produced, locked in for 20 years.
And the income was guaranteed for 20 years, even if the cost of electricity from other sources, and the wholesale price GRU could get for power from the rooftop arrays, fell sharply.
The cost pressures were compounded by other factors.
By 2014, when the program closed to new projects, Gainesville had added roughly 18 megawatts of solar.
But the program also has become part of a widely cited cautionary tale. Spain, which had greatly expanded its solar capacity under its FIT, then faced rising surcharges and cut its tariffs sharply. Germany, which had made the FIT model famous under its 2000 Renewable Energy Sources Act, also faced rising costs, and cut its tariffs sharply.
Gainesville officials, led by Regan, studied the German model and adapted it for a municipal utility.
It is stuck with its existing contracts, which will remain in place for two decades.
GRU capped new capacity at roughly 4 megawatts a year to control costs, and in some cases, it reduced the tariff for later participants, but the contracts early participants signed stayed locked in for two decades.
And there were other complaints.
The Gainesville program was modeled on Germany's feed-in tariff.
In the United States, the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act generally ties what utilities must pay small generators to their "avoided cost," meaning what the power would otherwise have cost them. Under federal law, wholesale power rates fall largely under the jurisdiction of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.
But GRU, which has been under pressure to control costs, capped new capacity at roughly 4 megawatts a year to control costs, and it has reduced the tariff for later participants, but the contracts early participants signed stay locked in for two decades.

# Gainesville's Feed-In Tariff and the Politics of Renewable Energy

In early 2009, Gainesville Regional Utilities (GRU), the city-owned power company in a north-central Florida college town, did something no American utility had done before. It offered anyone installing solar panels a guaranteed price for every kilowatt-hour produced, locked in for 20 years. The program was modeled on Germany's feed-in tariff, the policy credited with making a cloudy northern European country a global solar leader. For a few years, Gainesville became a pilgrimage site for clean-energy advocates.

## Borrowing from Germany

A feed-in tariff (FIT) offers a fixed, above-market rate under a long-term contract. The certainty lets homeowners, churches and small investors calculate returns in advance, and lets banks lend against predictable revenue. Led by strategic planner Ed Regan, Gainesville officials studied Germany's 2000 Renewable Energy Sources Act and adapted it. The initial rate was 32 cents per kilowatt-hour, several times what GRU paid for conventional power, with new capacity capped at roughly 4 megawatts a year. Demand was immediate: the first year's allotment filled almost at once, and commercial investors joined homeowners.

## The Advocate's View

Supporters saw proof that the policy could work in America. They argued FITs beat tax credits and rebates because they reward actual production, draw a broad range of participants, build a local installer workforce and lower costs through steady volume. By the time the program closed, Gainesville had added roughly 18 megawatts, placing it among national leaders by some per-capita measures.

## The Utility Executive's View

Inside a utility, the calculus differs. Above-market power is paid for by the broader ratepayer base. Gainesville's surcharge was modest, but critics noted that payers were often renters and lower-income residents, while returns went to property owners and investors, some from outside the city. Solar costs also fell faster than expected, so a reasonable 2009 rate looked generous later. GRU cut the tariff for later participants, but early contracts stayed locked in. Facing other cost pressures, including a controversial biomass plant contract, the city wound the program down, closing it to new applicants in 2014. The lesson many drew was that administratively fixed prices can drift out of step with a fast-moving market.

## The Analyst's View

Analysts cite structural reasons FITs stayed rare in the United States. First, jurisdiction: wholesale rates fall largely under the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, and the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act ties what utilities pay small generators to "avoided cost." State-mandated premiums risk conflict with that framework, while municipal utilities like GRU had more room to experiment. Second, most Americans are served by investor-owned utilities that profit from building infrastructure, so paying customers to generate power cuts against their model. They and their regulators prefer net metering, tax credits and renewable portfolio standards. Third, politics: Europe passed FITs within national strategies, while American policy is fragmented across 50 states and thousands of utilities, and bill subsidies invite charges of picking winners. Florida did not adopt the model statewide. Even in Europe, Germany and Spain faced rising surcharges and cut tariffs sharply, and many countries moved to competitive auctions.

## What Gainesville Leaves Behind

Gainesville is cited both as a success and a cautionary tale, and it was both. It showed guaranteed prices can rapidly unlock private investment, and that they can become costly when markets change faster than policy. The question it raises, who should bear the cost of the energy transition and who should share its rewards, remains live as utilities rewrite net metering rules and debate paying for rooftop solar and home batteries.
